text:
The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, developed under the Safe Surgery Saves Lives programme (2008) after extensive international consultation. It contains 19 items organized into three phases of the surgical pathway. A landmark multicenter study (New England Journal of Medicine, 2009) across eight hospitals worldwide reported that checklist implementation was associated with a reduction in the death rate from 1.5% to 0.8% and in inpatient complications from 11% to 7%. WHO permits reproduction of the checklist in its entirety; adapted versions should be labeled as based on the WHO checklist rather than carrying the WHO emblem.

SIGN IN — before induction of anaesthesia (with at least the nurse and the anaesthetist). Confirm: the patient has verified identity, surgical site, procedure and consent; the operative site is marked (or marking is not applicable); the anaesthesia machine and medication check is complete; the pulse oximeter is on the patient and functioning. Assess and confirm: known allergy status; difficult airway or aspiration risk, with equipment and assistance available if yes; risk of blood loss greater than 500 mL (greater than 7 mL/kg in children), with at least two intravenous lines or central access and fluids planned if yes.

TIME OUT — before skin incision (with nurse, anaesthetist and surgeon present). All team members introduce themselves by name and role. The team verbally confirms the patient's name, the procedure, and where the incision will be made. Antibiotic prophylaxis given within the last 60 minutes (or marked not applicable). Anticipated critical events are reviewed aloud: the surgeon states the critical or non-routine steps, how long the case will take, and the anticipated blood loss; the anaesthetist states any patient-specific concerns; the nursing team confirms sterility including indicator results and reports any equipment issues or concerns. Essential imaging is displayed as applicable.

SIGN OUT — before the patient leaves the operating room (with nurse, anaesthetist and surgeon). The nurse verbally confirms: the name of the procedure performed; completion of instrument, sponge and needle counts; specimen labelling read aloud including the patient name; whether any equipment problems need to be addressed. The surgeon, anaesthetist and nurse together review the key concerns for the patient's recovery and ongoing management.

Implementation notes. WHO recommends a single designated checklist coordinator (often the circulating nurse) to guide the process. The checklist is intentionally not comprehensive: additions and modifications to fit local practice are encouraged. NICE quality standard QS216 (based on NG180) includes completing the WHO surgical safety checklist for each surgical procedure as a quality statement. This summary paraphrases the 19 items; for the exact official wording and layout, consult the WHO source.
title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
